options.a: Keep the furniture and schedule a two-week flush-out before move-in instead of reviewing product emissions
options.b: Raise space temperature during occupied hours so the furniture off-gasses its formaldehyde faster
options.c: Select furniture verified for low formaldehyde emissions and increase ventilation during the transition
options.d: Upgrade the air-handler filters to MERV 13 so the formaldehyde is captured at the return grilles

distractorExplanations.a: A flush-out dilutes formaldehyde temporarily but leaves the emitting furniture in place; it is not source control.
distractorExplanations.b: Heating occupied space speeds emissions while people are present, increasing exposure instead of controlling the source.
distractorExplanations.d: MERV filters capture particles, not gases such as formaldehyde, so a filter upgrade does not address the emitting source.

options.a: It gives a direct reading of formaldehyde and other VOCs released by furniture and finishes in the room
options.b: It can indicate whether outdoor-air ventilation is keeping pace with occupant-generated contaminants
options.c: It confirms that supply air has passed through MERV 13 filtration before it reaches the meeting room
options.d: It detects incomplete combustion from nearby equipment before carbon monoxide reaches unsafe levels

distractorExplanations.a: CO2 sensors do not measure VOCs or formaldehyde; CO2 is only a proxy for occupant-related ventilation adequacy.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses ventilation with filtration: CO2 levels say nothing about filter efficiency, since filters do not remove CO2.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses carbon dioxide with carbon monoxide; combustion hazards require dedicated CO monitoring, not CO2 sensors.

options.a: Switch the air handlers to full economizer mode so stale indoor air is diluted with outdoor air more quickly
options.b: Run ozone-generating air purifiers on each occupied floor to neutralize smoke particles and lingering odours
options.c: Seal obvious envelope leaks, use appropriately rated particle filtration, and reduce outdoor-air intake only as allowed
options.d: Keep the standard MERV 8 filters in place and open operable windows to equalize indoor and outdoor pressure during the event

distractorExplanations.a: Full economizer mode pulls in more smoke-laden outdoor air during a wildfire event, raising indoor PM2.5 instead of lowering it.
distractorExplanations.b: Ozone generators do not remove particles and add a respiratory irritant that reacts with indoor chemicals to form new pollutants.
distractorExplanations.d: MERV 8 captures few fine smoke particles, and opening windows admits smoke directly, so indoor exposure would rise.

well-ap-readiness-check-air-water-nouris.explanation: During smoke events, a controlled approach combines filtration, envelope management and carefully adjusted ventilation consistent with health and code requirements. The goal is to limit particle ingress without creating unacceptable indoor-air conditions. Essential ventilation must still be maintained while outdoor-air intake is reduced.

options.a: VOCs are particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres, whereas particulate matter refers to gases released by combustion
options.b: VOCs are inorganic gases such as ozone and carbon monoxide, whereas particulate matter consists of organic vapours
options.c: VOCs are gases emitted from sources such as paints and cleaners, whereas particulate matter consists of suspended solid or liquid particles
options.d: VOCs are tracked with CO2 sensors as a ventilation proxy, whereas particulate matter is assessed by culturing airborne mould spores in a laboratory

distractorExplanations.a: Swaps the two definitions: PM2.5 describes particle size, while VOCs are gaseous organic compounds, not particles.
distractorExplanations.b: VOCs are organic compounds; ozone and CO are inorganic gases, and particulate matter is particles, not vapours.
distractorExplanations.d: CO2 sensors do not measure VOCs, and PM is measured by particle counters or gravimetric methods, not microbial culture.

options.a: Accept the manufacturer's laboratory claims and reduce outdoor-air ventilation in proportion to its stated clean-air rate
options.b: Confirm the device carries an electrical safety listing and treat that listing as proof of pathogen and particle removal
options.c: Run it in place of MERV 13 filtration, since ionization makes particles settle out of the breathing zone onto surfaces
options.d: Review independent evidence for effectiveness and verify that the device does not generate harmful ozone or by-products

distractorExplanations.a: Relying on vendor claims and cutting outdoor air removes a proven control before the device's real-world benefit is shown.
distractorExplanations.b: An electrical safety listing addresses shock and fire risk; it does not demonstrate air-cleaning effectiveness or by-products.
distractorExplanations.c: Ionization is not a substitute for rated filtration; particles deposited on surfaces can be resuspended and are not removed.

well-ap-readiness-check-air-water-nouris.explanation: Emerging air-cleaning technologies should be assessed for verified performance and unintended chemical by-products, particularly ozone. They complement rather than automatically replace source control, ventilation and filtration. That verification should reflect installed operating conditions, not only laboratory claims.

options.a: Approximately 5% to 15%
options.b: Approximately 15% to 25%
options.c: Approximately 30% to 60%
options.d: Approximately 65% to 85%

distractorExplanations.a: This range is far too dry; it causes eye, skin and mucous-membrane irritation and static discomfort for occupants.
distractorExplanations.b: Still below the commonly targeted 30% lower bound, so dryness complaints and irritation remain likely in winter.
distractorExplanations.d: Humidity above about 60% supports mould growth and dust mites, which is exactly what the target range is meant to avoid.

options.a: Treat the stain with a biocide and repaint with mould-resistant paint, then schedule the pipe repair for the next shutdown
options.b: Collect air samples for mould spores first and wait for laboratory results before deciding whether to repair the pipe
options.c: Stop the moisture source, dry affected materials promptly, and assess whether porous materials need removal or remediation
options.d: Increase supply airflow so the wet ceiling tile dries in place, and replace the pipe insulation at the next scheduled PM

distractorExplanations.a: Cosmetic treatment before stopping the leak leaves wet materials in place and allows microbial growth to continue.
distractorExplanations.b: Sampling is secondary; the first step is to stop the moisture source and dry materials, since mould can grow within 24-48 hours.
distractorExplanations.d: Drying in place without fixing the condensation source lets the tile re-wet, and porous materials may already need removal.

options.a: Install a carbon monoxide detector in the room, since the same sensor also alarms when radon levels are elevated
options.b: Test the drinking water for radon and treat the indoor air only if the water result exceeds the limit
options.c: Increase recirculation through MERV 13 filters, which capture radon gas before it reaches the breathing zone
options.d: Conduct radon testing using an accepted method and implement mitigation if results are elevated

distractorExplanations.a: CO detectors do not detect radon; radon requires dedicated short- or long-term radon testing with an accepted method.
distractorExplanations.b: Soil gas entering through the slab is the main radon pathway, so a water test cannot rule out an indoor-air problem.
distractorExplanations.c: Radon is a gas that passes through particle filters; mitigation relies on testing and measures such as sub-slab depressurization.

options.a: An occupied office with high CO2 readings during back-to-back meetings
options.b: An occupied area adjacent to fuel-burning equipment or an enclosed parking garage
options.c: A laboratory using electric hot plates and sealed reagent storage cabinets
options.d: A newly carpeted open office with elevated total VOC readings after the installation

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses carbon dioxide with carbon monoxide; high CO2 signals under-ventilation, not a combustion source that needs CO monitoring.
distractorExplanations.c: Electric heating produces no combustion by-products, so it is not a CO source; chemical storage calls for other controls.
distractorExplanations.d: Elevated TVOCs call for VOC source control and flush-out; carpet emissions do not produce carbon monoxide.

options.a: A recirculating range hood with a charcoal filter returning air to the room
options.b: A higher room air-change rate from the general HVAC supply diffusers
options.c: A properly designed and commissioned local exhaust hood vented outdoors
options.d: A portable HEPA air cleaner placed in the far corner of the classroom

distractorExplanations.a: A recirculating charcoal hood returns ultrafine particles and moisture to the room instead of exhausting them outdoors.
distractorExplanations.b: General dilution ventilation spreads contaminants through the room first; it does not capture them at the cooktop source.
distractorExplanations.d: A distant room air cleaner treats air after contaminants have spread; it is not local capture at the frying source.

options.a: To document the MERV rating needed for ventilation credit, since a filter log replaces outdoor-air verification
options.b: To verify that filtration performance is maintained and replacements occur before excessive loading compromises airflow
options.c: To track filter costs so replacement can be deferred until occupants report visible dust from the diffusers
options.d: To show that filters were changed once at construction completion, which satisfies the ongoing operations requirement for WELL

distractorExplanations.a: Filtration and outdoor-air delivery are separate requirements; a filter log does not verify ventilation rates.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting for visible dust means filters are already overloaded or bypassing; replacement should follow a planned schedule.
distractorExplanations.d: A single change at handover does not demonstrate ongoing maintenance; the log exists to track recurring replacements.

well-ap-readiness-check-air-water-nouris.explanation: A documented maintenance schedule helps ensure filters remain installed correctly and are changed when needed. Neglected filters can increase pressure drop, reduce delivered airflow and permit contaminant bypass if damaged or poorly seated. Overloaded or poorly seated filters also compromise bypass control.

options.a: Use low-emitting products first, isolate or schedule high-emitting work, then ventilate and flush out the space before occupancy
options.b: Ventilate and flush out the space first, then switch to low-emitting products on the next installation if TVOCs persist
options.c: Install portable air cleaners with HEPA filters and retest TVOCs, since particle filtration removes VOC emissions
options.d: Raise space temperature during occupied hours to accelerate off-gassing, then reduce ventilation once odours fade

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the hierarchy: source control through low-emitting products comes first, with ventilation and flush-out after.
distractorExplanations.c: HEPA filters capture particles, not gaseous VOCs, so this neither controls the source nor removes the measured TVOCs.
distractorExplanations.d: Heating during occupancy raises exposure, and cutting ventilation based on odour ignores measured TVOC levels.

options.a: Stagnation flushes sediment out of the service line, giving a cleaner baseline sample for comparison
options.b: Stagnation can reveal metals that leach from plumbing components into standing water
options.c: Stagnation lets the chlorine residual rise, which the laboratory needs before lead can be measured
options.d: Stagnation samples measure the lead level supplied by the utility at the water main before the building

distractorExplanations.a: Stagnation does the opposite: standing water picks up metals from plumbing; flushed samples, not stagnant ones, give a baseline.
distractorExplanations.c: Chlorine residual decays during stagnation, and lead analysis does not depend on residual disinfectant levels.
distractorExplanations.d: First-draw stagnant samples reflect the building's own fixtures and pipes, not the utility supply at the main.

options.a: Remove the fixture from service, provide safe alternative drinking water, investigate the source and remediate
options.b: Flush the fountain for two minutes each morning and keep it in use while a follow-up sample is scheduled
options.c: Install a carbon filter certified only for taste and odour, then return the fountain to use without any retesting
options.d: Post a notice asking pupils to run the water briefly and continue use until the annual sampling round

distractorExplanations.b: Daily flushing is a temporary measure that does not make an elevated-lead fixture safe for continued pupil use.
distractorExplanations.c: A taste-and-odour certification does not cover lead reduction, and returning it without retesting leaves the risk unverified.
distractorExplanations.d: Relying on pupils to flush and waiting for the next annual round leaves children exposed to a known lead result.

well-ap-readiness-check-air-water-nouris.explanation: Potentially contaminated fixtures should be taken out of service while the source is identified and corrected. Safe alternative access prevents an interruption in hydration while remediation and follow-up testing occur. The fixture returns to use only after remediation and confirmatory testing.

options.a: Provide subsidized bottled water at a central cafeteria that is open during the standard lunch hours on each weekday
options.b: Install one drinking fountain per floor beside the restrooms, without considering travel distance from desks
options.c: Provide free water stations in staff break rooms that are accessible to badge holders of a single department
options.d: Provide free, clearly marked potable-water stations within convenient travel distance of all regularly occupied areas

distractorExplanations.a: Paid, centralized water with limited hours creates cost and access barriers rather than free, convenient water.
distractorExplanations.b: A fixed count per floor can leave large areas far from water; equitable access is based on travel distance to occupied areas.
distractorExplanations.c: Limiting access to one department's badge holders excludes other regular occupants, which is not equitable access.

options.a: A filter-change indicator light on each station, which replaces the need for periodic water-quality testing
options.b: A one-time water test at commissioning, displayed as a certificate beside the station for the life of the building
options.c: A UV sanitizing lamp in the dispensing nozzle, used in place of a documented maintenance and cleaning schedule
options.d: A documented maintenance and testing programme with clear communication of the water source and service status

distractorExplanations.a: An indicator light only tracks filter life; it does not verify water quality or communicate the source and service status.
distractorExplanations.b: Water quality can change over time; trust depends on ongoing testing and maintenance, not a single handover result.
distractorExplanations.c: A UV nozzle lamp addresses surface microbes at the outlet but does not replace routine maintenance, testing or communication.

options.a: Shock-chlorinate the water heater once on reopening day and resume normal occupancy without further flushing
options.b: Lower the water heater setpoint during the closure to save energy, then flush the guest-room showers on the day of reopening
options.c: Test potable water for lead and copper before reopening, since metals testing also indicates Legionella risk
options.d: Follow a documented water management plan, including flushing, temperature control, inspections and corrective actions

distractorExplanations.a: A single shock treatment without flushing stagnant branch lines and ongoing control does not manage Legionella risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Lower hot-water temperatures during stagnation create Legionella growth conditions; flushing showers alone does not undo that.
distractorExplanations.c: Lead and copper results say nothing about Legionella; microbial risk needs a water management plan and targeted controls.

well-ap-readiness-check-air-water-nouris.explanation: Extended stagnation can create conditions favourable to Legionella. A risk-based water management plan addresses system recommissioning, temperature, disinfectant residuals, flushing and verification before occupants return. These steps should be completed before the hotel reopens to guests.

options.a: They keep hot water near 35 °C, which limits scalding risk and also stops Legionella growth
options.b: They remove the need for a water management plan once the circulating loop exceeds 50 °C
options.c: They help avoid long periods in temperature ranges that can support Legionella growth
options.d: They reduce lead leaching from old solder, which is the main way Legionella enters building water

distractorExplanations.a: Around 35 °C is close to the ideal Legionella growth range; control relies on keeping water outside roughly 20-50 °C.
distractorExplanations.b: Temperature control is one element of a water management plan; it does not replace monitoring, flushing and corrective actions.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses metals leaching with microbial risk; Legionella growth relates to temperature, stagnation and biofilm, not solder.

well-ap-readiness-check-air-water-nouris.explanation: Legionella control includes managing temperature throughout hot-water storage and distribution so water does not stagnate in a favourable growth range. Scald protection is handled separately at points of use. Delivery temperatures must still be managed to avoid scalding at outlets.

options.a: Certification that the filter meets taste and odour reduction claims, which also covers lead and microbial health contaminants
options.b: A manufacturer's in-house test report showing high contaminant removal at a flow rate above the rated capacity
options.c: Third-party certification that the specific filter reduces the target contaminant under its intended operating conditions
options.d: A filter with the smallest micron rating available, since pore size alone determines which chemicals are removed

distractorExplanations.a: Taste-and-odour (aesthetic) certification does not verify reduction of health contaminants such as lead or microbes.
distractorExplanations.b: An in-house report is not independent certification, and results above rated flow do not reflect intended operating conditions.
distractorExplanations.d: Micron rating describes particle capture; dissolved chemicals are removed by specific media, verified by contaminant-specific certification.

options.a: To prevent contaminated water from flowing backward into the drinking-water supply
options.b: To reduce excess pressure in the potable system so pipes and fixtures are not damaged
options.c: To keep hot water from cooling in the riser and creating Legionella growth conditions
options.d: To remove lead and copper particles before water reaches drinking fountains and taps

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a backflow preventer with a pressure-reducing valve, which limits supply pressure rather than preventing reverse flow.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes the purpose of hot-water recirculation, not a backflow device, which stops contaminated water reversing into potable lines.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses backflow prevention with point-of-use filtration; a backflow device does not treat or filter water.

options.a: Switch to stronger concentrated disinfectants so fountains can be cleaned less often between sampling rounds
options.b: Fill chemical dilution buckets at drinking fountains, which have better water quality than janitor's sinks
options.c: Rely on fountain bottle-filler filters to remove any cleaning-chemical residue left on the outlet surface after each cleaning
options.d: Train staff to use approved products and procedures and avoid storing or mixing chemicals near potable-water outlets

distractorExplanations.a: Stronger concentrates raise residue and exposure risk at outlets; the control is approved products, procedures and storage.
distractorExplanations.b: Filling or mixing chemicals at drinking outlets is precisely how cross-contamination occurs; use designated service sinks.
distractorExplanations.c: Filters treat water inside the unit, not chemical residue on the outlet surface, so they do not prevent contamination.

options.a: Add calorie counts to the menu board while keeping fried entrées as the featured default option at each station
options.b: Make fruits, vegetables and minimally processed options prominent, appealing and readily available
options.c: Replace sugar-sweetened beverages with diet soft drinks and keep the rest of the menu unchanged
options.d: Offer a weekly salad special while keeping desserts and chips at every checkout point

distractorExplanations.a: Labelling alone leaves the less healthy option as the default; Nourishment emphasizes making healthier foods prominent.
distractorExplanations.c: Swapping to diet drinks does not increase fruits, vegetables or minimally processed foods, which is the core menu shift.
distractorExplanations.d: An occasional special does not make healthy options readily available, and checkout confectionery keeps the unhealthy default.

options.a: Place a calorie-count poster at the exit while keeping the current product placement unchanged
options.b: Stop selling sugary drinks and stock only water and unsweetened tea instead
options.c: Place fruit, vegetables and water at eye level and at the start of the service line
options.d: Discount healthier items at the end of the line after trays are already filled

distractorExplanations.a: Information shown after choices are made does not nudge selection; placement at the point of choice does.
distractorExplanations.b: Removing products is a ban, which the question excludes; nudging changes placement and prominence, not availability.
distractorExplanations.d: Placing healthier items after trays are full reduces their influence; nudges work at eye level and the start of the line.

options.a: Provide clear nutrition and allergen information for standard menu items in a format employees can access before choosing
options.b: Post nutrition and allergen details on the company intranet once a year, even though the menu rotates every week
options.c: Display calorie counts at the register for standard items and give allergen details to diners only on request
options.d: Print detailed ingredient and allergen lists on receipts so employees can review the information after each purchase

distractorExplanations.b: Annually updated information goes out of date when menus rotate, so employees cannot rely on it when choosing meals.
distractorExplanations.c: Calories at the register come too late, and allergen details held by staff are not accessible to employees before choosing.
distractorExplanations.d: Receipt information arrives after the purchase, which defeats transparency meant to inform the choice beforehand.

options.a: Stock products chosen by employee vote each month, with no nutrition criteria applied to the final shortlist
options.b: Buy reduced-fat versions of current snacks, even where those versions contain more added sugar
options.c: Set purchasing standards that prioritise nutritious snacks and beverages while limiting high-sugar options
options.d: Offer free sugar-sweetened drinks as a staff perk while placing fruit in a paid vending machine

distractorExplanations.a: Preference voting without nutrition criteria does not ensure healthier availability; procurement standards are needed.
distractorExplanations.b: Reduced-fat products often add sugar, so this can worsen the high-sugar profile the policy is meant to limit.
distractorExplanations.d: Making sugary drinks free and fruit paid creates the opposite price incentive from healthier food availability.

well-ap-readiness-check-air-water-nouris.explanation: Procurement standards influence the default food environment. Prioritising nutritious offerings and limiting routine access to high-sugar products supports health without eliminating all individual choice. The aim is to limit routine availability of high-sugar items rather than ban them outright.

options.a: Allow branded energy-drink displays beside the water station if the vendor also funds a nutrition education poster nearby
options.b: Keep existing soda advertising but add calorie labels to the advertised products
options.c: Restrict marketing of highly processed, high-sugar foods while using the space to promote healthier options
options.d: Restrict advertising only during lunch periods while allowing sugary-drink ads at other times

distractorExplanations.a: Sponsorship of a poster does not offset marketing of high-sugar products, which WELL Nourishment seeks to restrict.
distractorExplanations.b: Labels do not remove promotional pressure; the principle is to restrict marketing of high-sugar, highly processed foods.
distractorExplanations.d: Students see ads throughout the day; time-limited restriction still markets high-sugar products in the cafeteria.

options.a: It satisfies the potable-water feature because the room includes a sink supplied with tested drinking water
options.b: It counts as a restorative space under Mind, so it can double as the building's quiet room
options.c: It provides a dedicated food-preparation area where infant formula is sold to employees
options.d: It supports breastfeeding and allows nursing parents to express and store milk safely and privately

distractorExplanations.a: A sink may be an amenity in the room, but the room's purpose is breastfeeding support, not meeting drinking-water features.
distractorExplanations.b: Sharing the room as a general quiet room undermines the privacy and availability that nursing parents need.
distractorExplanations.c: A lactation room supports expressing and storing breast milk; it is not a retail or food-preparation space.

options.a: Raised planters of ornamental grasses with signage about local plant species
options.b: A programme for growing edible produce with safe soil and water practices
options.c: Edible plants grown in reclaimed soil without testing, open to anyone at any time
options.d: A vegetable plot maintained by contractors whose harvest is sold off site

distractorExplanations.a: Ornamental planting with signage is landscape and biophilia, not food production, so it is not a nourishment intervention.
distractorExplanations.c: Untested soil can carry lead or other contaminants, so produce grown this way lacks the safe soil practices required.
distractorExplanations.d: If occupants neither use the produce nor engage with the garden, it does not function as an occupant nourishment strategy.

well-ap-readiness-check-air-water-nouris.explanation: A nourishment garden should support safe cultivation, learning or access to edible food. Soil safety, irrigation quality, integrated pest management and participant guidance are important implementation details. Access rules and education or use by occupants complete a credible garden programme.

options.a: Identify the pest and eliminate food, water, entry and harborage conditions through sanitation and exclusion
options.b: Apply a broad-spectrum pesticide on a fixed monthly schedule as a preventive barrier in each prep area
options.c: Set bait stations first and review sanitation only if pest sightings continue after three months
options.d: Fog the kitchen after hours with a residual insecticide, then wipe the food-contact surfaces before opening the next day

distractorExplanations.b: Calendar-based spraying is the opposite of IPM, which applies pesticides only after identification and non-chemical controls.
distractorExplanations.c: IPM starts with identification, sanitation and exclusion; baiting first and delaying sanitation reverses that order.
distractorExplanations.d: Fogging is a high-exposure chemical step that IPM reserves for last, after the conditions supporting pests are removed.

options.a: Switch to a stronger quaternary ammonium spray applied less often, keeping the aerosol method unchanged
options.b: Keep daily aerosol spraying but schedule it at noon, when outdoor-air ventilation rates are at their peak
options.c: Replace disinfection with fragrance-free air fresheners, since odour control is the main WELL cleaning goal
options.d: Use a risk-based cleaning protocol with lower-emitting products and targeted application methods

distractorExplanations.a: Stronger quats sprayed as aerosols still create inhalation exposure; the fix is lower-emitting products and targeted application.
distractorExplanations.b: Spraying at noon exposes occupants during peak occupancy; higher ventilation does not remove the aerosol source.
distractorExplanations.c: Air fresheners add emissions and do not disinfect; WELL cleaning aims to reduce exposure while keeping necessary disinfection.

well-ap-readiness-check-air-water-nouris.explanation: Effective hygiene does not require indiscriminate aerosolisation. Targeted, documented cleaning with safer products and appropriate ventilation reduces unnecessary respiratory exposure while preserving sanitation. Required disinfection is still performed where the risk warrants it.

options.a: Ozone can irritate the respiratory system and react with indoor chemicals to form additional pollutants
options.b: Ozone breaks down quickly into oxygen, so its main concern is reduced filter life in the AHU
options.c: Ozone raises indoor CO2 levels, which forces the ventilation system to bring in more outdoor air to compensate
options.d: Ozone removes VOCs effectively, but it can bleach fabrics and finishes after prolonged exposure

distractorExplanations.b: Ozone persists long enough indoors to harm occupants; the primary concern is respiratory irritation, not filter life.
distractorExplanations.c: Ozone does not produce CO2; its concerns are respiratory irritation and reactions forming secondary pollutants.
distractorExplanations.d: Ozone reacts with VOCs to create new pollutants such as formaldehyde rather than removing them, and harms people first.

options.a: A UV-C lamp inside the unit, since ultraviolet light removes particles from the airstream
options.b: A clean air delivery rate appropriate for the room size, with no harmful ozone production
options.c: The highest fan airflow in cubic feet per minute, even with a low-efficiency mesh filter
options.d: An ionizer setting that charges particles so they settle on nearby room surfaces

distractorExplanations.a: UV-C can inactivate microbes but does not capture particles; particle control depends on filtration and CADR.
distractorExplanations.c: Raw airflow is not clean air delivery; CADR combines airflow with filter efficiency, so a mesh filter yields little.
distractorExplanations.d: Settled particles are not removed and can be resuspended, and ionizers may emit ozone, which the key excludes.

options.a: Run the HVAC on full recirculation for 24 hours, then reoccupy once visible dust is no longer present
options.b: Replace the air-handler filters after reoccupation, since filter loading is the best sign that dust has been removed
options.c: Conduct documented post-construction cleaning and, where required, verify airborne contaminants through appropriate testing
options.d: Rely on the contractor's verbal confirmation of cleaning and measure CO2 levels on the first day of occupancy

distractorExplanations.a: Recirculation spreads construction dust, and visual checks cannot confirm fine particles have been cleaned or removed.
distractorExplanations.b: Changing filters after people return does not verify the space is clean; documented cleaning and testing come before reoccupation.
distractorExplanations.d: Verbal assurance is not documentation, and CO2 indicates ventilation rather than construction dust or airborne contaminants.

options.a: Indoor relative humidity held near 35% during winter, with continuous exhaust running in the bathrooms and kitchens
options.b: A vapour-open wall assembly that lets small amounts of moisture dry toward the exterior
options.c: Persistent condensation on cold surfaces due to uncontrolled humid indoor air and thermal bridges
options.d: Short-term high humidity during a summer storm in a building with an intact air barrier

distractorExplanations.a: Moderate winter humidity with wet-room exhaust is a moisture control measure, not a cause of envelope microbial growth.
distractorExplanations.b: Vapour-open assemblies allow drying, which reduces rather than causes moisture accumulation in the envelope.
distractorExplanations.d: Brief humidity spikes with an intact air barrier rarely cause growth; persistent condensation on cold surfaces does.

options.a: Cooling-tower drift releases lead particles that settle in nearby drinking-water outlets
options.b: Cooling towers raise indoor CO2 when their plume is drawn back into outdoor-air intakes
options.c: Poorly controlled cooling towers can amplify and disseminate Legionella-containing aerosols
options.d: Cooling-tower water mixes with the domestic hot-water loop, which spreads Legionella to taps

distractorExplanations.a: Cooling-tower health risk is Legionella in drift aerosols; towers are not a lead source for drinking-water outlets.
distractorExplanations.b: Plume re-entrainment matters because of Legionella aerosols, not CO2; cooling-tower water does not generate CO2.
distractorExplanations.d: Condenser water and domestic water are separate systems; the tower risk is aerosol dissemination of Legionella.

options.a: It makes hydration convenient at a point where people may be physically active or passing through regularly
options.b: It allows the project to omit drinking water on upper floors because the stairwell station serves the building
options.c: It helps meet the Thermal Comfort concept by cooling occupants who use the stairs during summer
options.d: It replaces separate drinking-fountain maintenance because fitness staff can test the station weekly

distractorExplanations.b: One well-placed station does not replace convenient water access near the other regularly occupied areas.
distractorExplanations.c: Hydration placement supports Water and Movement goals; it is not a Thermal Comfort strategy for cooling occupants.
distractorExplanations.d: Placement does not change maintenance obligations; every potable outlet still needs documented upkeep and testing.

options.a: The arrangement is acceptable if calorie labels are posted on each beverage at the checkout cooler
options.b: The arrangement mainly breaches food-safety rules because beverages must be stored away from the register
options.c: The arrangement is acceptable if the water is free, since price alone determines WELL beverage compliance
options.d: The arrangement makes the less healthy default most convenient and creates an unnecessary barrier to water access

distractorExplanations.a: Labels do not fix the problem that the unhealthy option is the convenient default while water is hidden.
distractorExplanations.b: The WELL Nourishment issue is choice architecture and water access, not a food-safety storage rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Free water kept in a back room is still a barrier; visibility and convenience matter alongside price.

options.a: A vegan meal served in large portions and labelled 'healthy', but with no ingredient or allergen information posted
options.b: A low-calorie salad with calorie counts listed, but with no protein option or allergen labelling for diners
options.c: A clearly labelled vegetable-forward meal with whole-grain and protein options, including ingredient and allergen information
options.d: A gluten-free meal offered on request, with ingredients listed on a sheet that is kept in the kitchen

distractorExplanations.a: A plant-based label is not enough; without ingredient and allergen information, the meal is not inclusive or transparent.
distractorExplanations.b: Calorie counts alone omit allergen information and balanced protein options, so the offering is neither complete nor inclusive.
distractorExplanations.d: Information held in the kitchen is not accessible at the point of choice, and an on-request meal is not a standard offering.

options.a: Replace the diffusers with a style that throws air away from desks so the dust is less visible to occupants
options.b: Inspect filter fit and replacement history, duct cleanliness and sources of particle generation
options.c: Increase the outdoor-air rate, since visible dust from diffusers indicates that CO2 levels in the zone are too high
options.d: Schedule duct cleaning across the whole building at once, before checking filters or local dust sources

distractorExplanations.a: Changing diffuser throw hides the symptom; the investigation should find where the particles enter or bypass filtration.
distractorExplanations.c: Visible dust is a particle and filtration problem; it does not indicate elevated CO2 or under-ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: Building-wide duct cleaning before diagnosis is costly and may not fix a filter bypass or nearby construction source.

well-ap-readiness-check-air-water-nouris.explanation: Visible dust warrants a systematic review of filtration installation, maintenance, source control and possible construction contamination. The response should identify the particulate source rather than mask it. Construction dust controls should be checked as part of the same investigation.

options.a: To confirm the design calculations meet code, which removes the need to measure airflow after installation
options.b: To confirm that the installed system delivers the intended outdoor air to occupied zones under operating conditions
options.c: To set the filter MERV rating, since outdoor-air rate commissioning is mainly a filtration requirement
options.d: To record the outdoor-air damper position at the AHU, which proves the airflow reaching each occupied zone

distractorExplanations.a: Design review is not commissioning; commissioning measures what the installed system actually delivers in operation.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses filtration with ventilation; outdoor-air commissioning verifies airflow quantity, not filter efficiency.
distractorExplanations.d: Damper position does not prove delivered airflow; zone-level measurement under operating conditions is needed.

options.a: Ventilation for occupancy may be adequate, but source emissions still require investigation and control
options.b: Low CO2 shows the TVOC sensor is faulty, since both readings rise and fall together with the number of occupants
options.c: TVOC levels will fall on their own once CO2 rises, so no source investigation is required
options.d: The outdoor-air rate should be reduced because low CO2 shows the space is over-ventilated

distractorExplanations.b: TVOCs come largely from materials and products, not people, so they can be high while occupant-driven CO2 is low.
distractorExplanations.c: Rising CO2 means less ventilation per person, which would tend to raise TVOCs; post-renovation sources still need review.
distractorExplanations.d: Cutting ventilation while renovation emissions are elevated would increase TVOC exposure rather than address the source.

options.a: Use dry dusting with feather dusters every day so that particles are removed more often
options.b: Use standard bag vacuums during occupied hours so the cleaning is visible to staff
options.c: Use HEPA-filtered vacuuming and damp wiping methods according to a routine schedule
options.d: Use leaf blowers in corridors after hours and reoccupy the space the next morning

distractorExplanations.a: Dry dusting lifts settled particles back into the air; damp wiping captures them instead of resuspending them.
distractorExplanations.b: Non-HEPA vacuums exhaust fine particles, and cleaning during occupancy increases occupant exposure to resuspended dust.
distractorExplanations.d: Blowers resuspend dust that later resettles on surfaces occupants touch; they move particles rather than remove them.

options.a: Rely on transfer air from the adjacent corridor and add portable air cleaners to make up for the lack of operable windows
options.b: Install a high-capacity recirculating fan coil with MERV 13 filters, which counts as outdoor-air ventilation
options.c: Mechanically provide and verify required outdoor airflow, control pollutant sources and monitor relevant indoor-air conditions
options.d: Provide outdoor air at the design rate on paper and measure CO2 once at handover without ongoing monitoring

distractorExplanations.a: Transfer air is not outdoor air, and portable cleaners do not supply ventilation; the studio needs verified outdoor airflow.
distractorExplanations.b: Recirculated, filtered air does not dilute CO2 or gaseous contaminants; it does not count as outdoor-air ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: A design figure plus one handover reading neither verifies delivered airflow nor tracks indoor-air conditions in use.

options.a: It lets the team sample high-risk fixtures alone, since representative outlets just repeat the utility report
options.b: It allows the lab to composite samples from many outlets into one result for the whole building
options.c: It replaces the need for a water management plan by covering every fixture type once at handover
options.d: It helps characterize overall water quality while detecting localized problems

distractorExplanations.a: Representative outlets show building-wide quality that utility data cannot; dropping them loses the overall picture.
distractorExplanations.b: Compositing dilutes a single bad outlet into an average and hides exactly the localized problems sampling should find.
distractorExplanations.c: A sampling plan is one input to water management; one-time sampling at handover does not replace an ongoing plan.

well-ap-readiness-check-air-water-nouris.explanation: Water quality can vary across a plumbing system. Sampling a representative set and targeted high-risk locations provides a more useful assessment than testing only one convenient outlet. Localized problems are often caused by specific plumbing materials or low-use conditions.

options.a: Top up the pans with fresh food on top of existing food to reduce waste during long service periods
options.b: Rely on sneeze guards at the bar, since they remove the need for cold-holding temperature checks
options.c: Maintain required cold-holding temperatures and implement hygiene, cleaning and replenishment procedures
options.d: Check food temperatures once at opening and rely on fast turnover for the rest of the service day

distractorExplanations.a: Layering fresh food over older food extends holding time and spreads contamination; pans should be replaced, not topped up.
distractorExplanations.b: Sneeze guards limit contamination from customers but do not control bacterial growth; temperature control is still required.
distractorExplanations.d: A single check cannot show foods stay at safe cold-holding temperatures; monitoring must continue through service.

options.a: Provide a private restroom stall with a chair for expressing milk during scheduled breaks
options.b: Offer unpaid leave extensions in place of on-site break time and space for employees who are breastfeeding
options.c: Allow milk expression in a shared first-aid room that doubles as a storage area for supplies
options.d: Provide reasonable break time and a private, non-toilet lactation space with appropriate amenities

distractorExplanations.a: A toilet area is unhygienic for expressing milk; lactation space must be private and not a bathroom.
distractorExplanations.b: Extended leave does not support employees who have returned to work; they need break time and a lactation space.
distractorExplanations.c: A shared first-aid or storage room cannot guarantee the privacy and availability a dedicated lactation space provides.

options.a: Locate fire-rated egress stairs at the building core and add signs pointing to them from the lobby
options.b: Place attractive, visible stairs near main circulation and reduce reliance on elevators for short trips
options.c: Provide a fitness room on the top floor and keep the stairs enclosed behind closed doors for building security
options.d: Install faster destination-dispatch elevators so occupants spend less time waiting between floors

distractorExplanations.a: Enclosed egress stairs at the core are rarely attractive or visible; signs alone do not create an inviting stair.
distractorExplanations.c: A fitness room does not encourage daily stair use, and hidden enclosed stairs push occupants toward elevators.
distractorExplanations.d: Faster elevators make the sedentary option more convenient, which works against Movement goals for short trips.

options.a: Percentage of occupants predicted to be dissatisfied with the space
options.b: Mean radiant temperature of the surfaces surrounding an occupant
options.c: Metabolic rate of occupants expressed in met units for each activity
options.d: Predicted mean vote of thermal sensation on a comfort scale

distractorExplanations.a: That describes PPD (Predicted Percentage Dissatisfied), which is derived from PMV but is a separate index.
distractorExplanations.b: Mean radiant temperature is one input to the PMV calculation, not what the PMV index itself represents.
distractorExplanations.c: Metabolic rate (met) is an input to PMV alongside clothing, air temperature, radiant temperature, air speed and humidity.

options.a: Lower melanopic content and illuminance during night shifts while maintaining task visibility
options.b: Raise melanopic content during night shifts to keep workers alert, then dim the lighting at sunrise
options.c: Keep a constant 4000 K at full output around the clock so day and night shifts see equal light
options.d: Switch to blue-enriched 6500 K lighting overnight but at half the daytime illuminance level

distractorExplanations.b: High melanopic light at night suppresses melatonin and shifts the circadian clock, increasing disruption.
distractorExplanations.c: Constant bright light removes day-night contrast, so night workers still receive circadian-disrupting exposure.
distractorExplanations.d: Halving illuminance does not offset the high melanopic ratio of 6500 K light, which still disrupts circadian rhythm at night.

options.a: PMV/PPD model with fixed clothing and metabolic inputs, as used for sealed air-conditioned offices
options.b: Adaptive comfort model with narrower acceptable ranges, since window use makes conditions less stable
options.c: Mean radiant temperature limits from the local discomfort section, applied in place of a comfort model
options.d: Adaptive comfort model allowing wider acceptable temperature ranges when users can adjust openings

distractorExplanations.a: PMV/PPD suits mechanically conditioned spaces; occupant-controlled naturally ventilated spaces fit the adaptive model.
distractorExplanations.b: The adaptive model allows wider, not narrower, acceptable temperatures because occupants can adapt and control openings.
distractorExplanations.c: Local discomfort limits supplement an overall comfort model; they are not a substitute framework for naturally ventilated spaces.

options.a: Permanently fritted glazing at 80% coverage, applied uniformly on every facade
options.b: Interior blackout roller blinds that occupants lower fully whenever glare appears
options.c: Automated or manual shades that block direct sun while preserving diffuse daylight
options.d: Dark-tinted glass with 10% visible transmittance on all orientations without shades

distractorExplanations.a: Dense fixed frit cuts useful daylight on every orientation and cannot respond to changing sun position.
distractorExplanations.b: Fully lowered blackout blinds remove daylight along with glare; the aim is to block direct sun but keep diffuse light.
distractorExplanations.d: Very low visible transmittance sacrifices daylight access and still offers no adjustable control of direct sun.

options.a: To measure horizontal task illuminance on the desk surface for reading and keyboard work
options.b: To calculate annual sunlight exposure (ASE) across the floor plate as an indicator of glare risk
options.c: To evaluate light available for visual and circadian effects at the occupant's line of sight
options.d: To verify luminaire efficacy in lumens per watt against the allowed lighting power density

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses horizontal task illuminance with vertical illuminance at the eye, which determines circadian light exposure.
distractorExplanations.b: ASE is an annual horizontal grid metric for overlit area; it is not a measurement at the occupant's eye.
distractorExplanations.d: Efficacy and lighting power density are energy metrics; they do not describe light reaching the occupant's eye.

options.a: Survey occupants and check local radiant asymmetry, air speed, and solar gains at complaint locations
options.b: Recalibrate the central thermostat and raise supply airflow to the whole zone before speaking to occupants
options.c: Lower the zone setpoint by two degrees for a week and log whether the number of complaints drops
options.d: Move the thermostat into the return-air plenum so it reads the average zone temperature more accurately

distractorExplanations.b: Zone-wide changes ignore that complaints are local; radiant, air-speed and solar causes must be diagnosed where they occur.
distractorExplanations.c: Changing the setpoint without diagnosis may help hot complaints and worsen cold ones; local conditions need checking first.
distractorExplanations.d: A plenum reading still hides local radiant asymmetry and drafts at desks, which explain mixed hot-cold complaints.

options.a: Warm 2700 K lighting during the day to reduce eye strain and match residential settings
options.b: Neutral to cool-white spectrum with adequate melanopic content during working hours
options.c: Cool 6500 K lighting at maximum output in the morning and evening, dimmed at midday
options.d: Low-intensity lighting below 150 lux with high color rendering for visual comfort

distractorExplanations.a: Warm 2700 K light has low melanopic content, which provides weaker daytime circadian stimulus for alertness.
distractorExplanations.c: Bright cool light in the evening delays the circadian clock; strong melanopic light belongs in daytime working hours.
distractorExplanations.d: Good color rendering does not offset very low illuminance, which gives little melanopic stimulus for daytime alertness.

options.a: Thermal Comfort and occupant thermal control options
options.b: Community and universal design for site access
options.c: Movement and related active transportation support
options.d: Water and access to hygiene and handwashing

distractorExplanations.a: Showers serve commuters who arrive after active travel; they are not a strategy for controlling indoor temperature.
distractorExplanations.b: Universal design concerns accessibility for people of different abilities, not facilities for cycling commuters.
distractorExplanations.d: Showers here support active commuting under Movement; Water hygiene features address handwashing and water quality.

options.a: Higher risk of mould growth on cold window frames and wall surfaces
options.b: Increased dust mite populations in carpets and upholstered seating
options.c: Higher perceived warmth leading to more overheating complaints
options.d: Dry air discomfort affecting eyes and respiratory mucous membranes

distractorExplanations.a: Mould growth is linked to high humidity and condensation; 18% RH is too dry to support it.
distractorExplanations.b: Dust mites thrive in humid conditions; very low winter humidity suppresses them rather than increasing them.
distractorExplanations.c: Low humidity increases evaporative cooling of the skin, so occupants tend to feel cooler, not warmer.

options.a: PMV and PPD (Predicted Percentage Dissatisfied)
options.b: MRT and SHGC (Solar Heat Gain Coefficient)
options.c: EML and CCT (Equivalent Melanopic Lux, Color Temperature)
options.d: sDA and ASE (Annual Sunlight Exposure)

distractorExplanations.b: Mean radiant temperature is a PMV input and SHGC is a glazing property; neither pair expresses acceptability under ASHRAE 55.
distractorExplanations.c: EML and CCT are lighting metrics used in WELL Light, not thermal comfort indices from ASHRAE 55.
distractorExplanations.d: sDA and ASE are daylighting metrics from IES LM-83, not ASHRAE 55 thermal acceptability measures.

options.a: Occupancy sensing will switch lights off during meetings because photocells cannot detect motion
options.b: Daylight harvesting will dim lights incorrectly because sensors do not see perimeter daylight conditions
options.c: Lights will flicker at visible frequencies because photocells change the LED driver output
options.d: Circadian tuning will fail because photocells set the colour temperature of each fixture

distractorExplanations.a: Photocells sense light levels, not occupancy; occupancy control uses separate motion or presence sensors.
distractorExplanations.c: Flicker depends on driver design; photocell placement affects daylight response, not flicker frequency.
distractorExplanations.d: Photocells used for daylight harvesting control dimming level; tunable spectrum is set by separate controls.

options.a: Provide high-quality electric lighting with appropriate spectrum, intensity, and glare control at workstations
options.b: Install tubular daylight devices only in perimeter zones, where occupants already receive window daylight
options.c: Raise horizontal desk illuminance to 1,000 lux with warm 2700 K lamps to make up for missing daylight
options.d: Provide light-therapy lamps on request while keeping standard overhead lighting with bare lamps in view

distractorExplanations.b: Placing daylight devices at the perimeter helps those who already have windows, not interior occupants lacking daylight.
distractorExplanations.c: More horizontal light from warm lamps adds glare risk and gives weak melanopic stimulus at the eye for interior occupants.
distractorExplanations.d: Ad hoc therapy lamps do not fix base lighting quality, and exposed bare lamps create glare at workstations.

options.a: Radiant temperature difference from solar-heated glazing while air temperature remains moderate
options.b: Stratified supply air from overhead diffusers pooling warm air near the ceiling of the perimeter zone
options.c: High relative humidity near the glazing raising the perceived air temperature at the desk
options.d: Excess outdoor air from the economizer cooling the space below setpoint near the facade

distractorExplanations.b: Stratification causes vertical temperature differences, not one-sided discomfort facing a sunny glass wall.
distractorExplanations.c: Winter humidity is usually low, and humidity affects whole-body comfort rather than one-sided radiant asymmetry.
distractorExplanations.d: Over-cooling by outdoor air lowers air temperature evenly; the scenario states air temperature remains moderate.

options.a: Higher color rendering index than fixed-white LEDs, which is the main circadian lighting metric
options.b: Elimination of glare from luminaires, since tunable-white fixtures have lower surface luminance
options.c: Reduced flicker at all dimming levels, which WELL treats as the core purpose of tunable fixtures
options.d: Ability to adjust spectrum and intensity across the day to support circadian and visual needs

distractorExplanations.a: CRI describes color fidelity; circadian lighting in WELL is measured with melanopic metrics such as EML.
distractorExplanations.b: Tunable spectrum does not reduce luminaire luminance; glare control depends on optics, shielding and placement.
distractorExplanations.c: Flicker performance depends on the driver; tunable-white fixtures exist to vary spectrum and intensity over the day.

options.a: Excessive radiant asymmetry from the retail glazing reaching the upper floors
options.b: Zone load diversity and inadequate local control for dissimilar occupancies
options.c: Low clothing insulation among retail staff compared with office workers
options.d: Stack effect drawing cold outdoor air down through the office floors

distractorExplanations.a: Radiant effects from ground-floor glazing do not reach upper floors; the issue is one system serving unlike loads.
distractorExplanations.c: Clothing differences cannot explain cold upper floors; a single air system cannot satisfy dissimilar zone loads.
distractorExplanations.d: Stack effect in heating season draws cold air in at lower levels, so it would not explain a warm ground floor.

options.a: Spatial Daylight Autonomy (sDA) or similar area-based daylight metrics
options.b: Annual Sunlight Exposure (ASE) measuring the overlit area from direct sun
options.c: Daylight factor measured at a single point under overcast sky
options.d: Unified Glare Rating (UGR) for luminaires in the occupied zone

distractorExplanations.b: ASE flags area receiving too much direct sun (glare and heat risk), not area meeting minimum daylight thresholds.
distractorExplanations.c: Daylight factor is a point ratio under one sky condition, not a climate-based area percentage over the year.
distractorExplanations.d: UGR rates discomfort glare from electric luminaires and says nothing about daylight sufficiency across floor area.

options.a: Meets Light circadian targets in stairwells and reduces the energy used by elevator travel
options.b: Encourages stair use (Movement) and improves perceived safety and comfort in circulation
options.c: Satisfies Materials ingredient disclosure and improves acoustic privacy in circulation
options.d: Counts toward Mind restorative space and replaces the need for active furnishings

distractorExplanations.a: Signage and finishes do not deliver circadian lighting targets; the benefits are stair use and perceived safety.
distractorExplanations.c: Attractive finishes do not equal ingredient disclosure, and stair design is not an acoustic privacy strategy.
distractorExplanations.d: A stairwell is circulation, not a restorative space, and stair use does not replace active workstations.

options.a: A unit describing the metabolic heat output of seated occupants
options.b: A measure of radiant heat transfer between occupants and nearby glazing
options.c: A unit describing insulating value of occupant clothing ensembles
options.d: A factor describing local air speed at the occupant's ankles

distractorExplanations.a: Metabolic heat output is expressed in met units, not clo, which measures clothing insulation.
distractorExplanations.b: Radiant exchange is captured by mean radiant temperature, a separate PMV input from clothing insulation (clo).
distractorExplanations.d: Ankle air speed is a draft and local discomfort parameter, measured in m/s or fpm, not in clo.

options.a: Mechanical setpoint widening that removes the need for occupant comfort surveys
options.b: Personal adaptation through clothing adjustment within acceptable environmental limits
options.c: Metabolic rate adjustment through activity changes during the working day
options.d: Radiant comfort control through personal heaters at every workstation

distractorExplanations.a: Dress flexibility lets people adapt; it does not change setpoints or remove the need to survey occupant comfort.
distractorExplanations.c: The policy changes clothing insulation (clo), not activity level or metabolic rate (met).
distractorExplanations.d: Personal heaters are a personal comfort system; a dress policy relies on clothing adjustment instead.

options.a: Gradually reduce melanopic content and illuminance after sunset while maintaining safe egress lighting
options.b: Keep daytime 5000 K settings until the building closes, then switch directly to egress lighting
options.c: Raise melanopic content in the evening to counter end-of-day fatigue among late-working staff
options.d: Dim illuminance after sunset but shift to cooler 6500 K so screens appear sharper to occupants

distractorExplanations.b: Holding daytime spectrum into the evening gives late workers high melanopic exposure before an abrupt cut.
distractorExplanations.c: Evening melanopic boosts suppress melatonin and delay sleep timing, which is the opposite of circadian-friendly.
distractorExplanations.d: Shifting to cooler 6500 K raises the melanopic ratio, partly undoing the circadian benefit of dimming in the evening.

options.a: Diffuse electric light from perimeter luminaires toward the building core
options.b: Block daylight from reaching the core to reduce glare on interior screens
options.c: Reduce the window-to-wall ratio needed to meet energy code requirements
options.d: Reflect daylight deeper into the space while shading direct sun near the window

distractorExplanations.a: Light shelves are passive daylight devices; they do not redirect electric light from luminaires.
distractorExplanations.b: Light shelves redirect daylight deeper into the plan rather than keeping it away from the core.
distractorExplanations.c: Light shelves do not change the window-to-wall ratio; they redistribute daylight from existing glazing.

options.a: Provide adjustable diffusers, fans, or zoning where feasible within acceptable environmental bounds
options.b: Set a single building-wide setpoint at the mean preferred temperature from the occupant survey
options.c: Widen the deadband between heating and cooling so the system responds less to complaints
options.d: Provide personal heaters on request and keep the zone thermostat locked at a fixed setting

distractorExplanations.b: A mean setpoint still leaves people at either end of the preference range uncomfortable; local control addresses differences.
distractorExplanations.c: A wider deadband saves energy but reduces responsiveness and does nothing for individual temperature preferences.
distractorExplanations.d: Ad hoc heaters address only cold complaints, and a locked thermostat removes adjustment for those who run warm.

options.a: EML depends on the sun's angle, so readings must be adjusted to an equivalent solar-noon value before comparison
options.b: Circadian-effective light targets vary by time of day to support appropriate day-night entrainment
options.c: EML is measured on the horizontal plane, so morning sun distorts the horizontal reading
options.d: Morning readings include electric light, while WELL counts daylight only in EML values

distractorExplanations.a: EML is not normalized to noon; WELL compares readings with time-of-day targets for circadian entrainment.
distractorExplanations.c: EML for circadian assessment is measured vertically at the eye, not on the horizontal work plane.
distractorExplanations.d: EML counts melanopic light from any source, daylight or electric, measured at the eye.

options.a: Placing a printer and kitchenette within each team's desk cluster to save time between tasks
options.b: Installing faster elevators so trips between floors take less time for office workers
options.c: Centralizing shared amenities such as printers, mail, and break areas away from every desk cluster
options.d: Providing height-adjustable desks at every workstation while keeping amenities nearby

distractorExplanations.a: Distributed amenities reduce walking; centralizing them increases short daily trips that support Movement.
distractorExplanations.b: Faster elevators shorten sedentary travel and discourage stair walking rather than adding steps.
distractorExplanations.d: Sit-stand desks reduce sitting time but do not add walking distance, which depends on amenity placement.

options.a: Relative humidity in the return-air plenum
options.b: Mean radiant temperature of the exterior wall surface
options.c: Outdoor-air fraction at the air-handling unit
options.d: Air speed and diffuser throw at occupant locations

distractorExplanations.a: Return-plenum humidity does not explain localized drafts; draft complaints relate to air speed at occupants.
distractorExplanations.b: Radiant asymmetry is a different discomfort mechanism; drafts from an overhead diffuser point to air speed and throw.
distractorExplanations.c: Outdoor-air fraction affects ventilation, not the local air velocity occupants feel beneath a diffuser.

options.a: High SHGC with low visible light transmittance on south and west facades
options.b: Low solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC) with adequate visible light transmittance
options.c: Low U-factor alone, which limits both solar heat gain and visible daylight transmission
options.d: Dark-tinted glass with low visible transmittance to block both heat and glare

distractorExplanations.a: This combination admits more solar heat while cutting daylight, the reverse of the desired performance.
distractorExplanations.c: U-factor measures conductive heat loss; it does not control solar gain or daylight transmission.
distractorExplanations.d: Dark tints cut daylight along with heat; spectrally selective low-SHGC glass preserves visible light.

options.a: Restorative design and stress-reduction features under Mind
options.b: Ergonomic workstation requirements under Thermal Comfort
options.c: Active design and behavioral prompts supporting Movement
options.d: Health promotion and civic engagement under Community

distractorExplanations.a: Standing tables and stair prompts target physical activity under Movement, not restoration or stress reduction.
distractorExplanations.b: Ergonomics sits under Movement in WELL v2, and these prompts encourage activity rather than set ergonomic specs.
distractorExplanations.d: Civic engagement concerns occupant participation in the community; stair prompts and standing tables are active design.

options.a: High air speed from supply diffusers mounted in the ceiling above the main sales floor
options.b: Low relative humidity at floor level from winter heating of the sales area
options.c: Excess radiant heat from display lighting directed toward the floor surface
options.d: Low mean radiant temperature at the floor surface despite moderate air temperature

distractorExplanations.a: Ceiling diffuser drafts cause neck and head complaints; cold feet on a slab point to floor surface temperature.
distractorExplanations.b: Humidity does not vary meaningfully at floor level and is not what makes a slab floor feel cold underfoot.
distractorExplanations.c: Radiant heat from lighting would warm the floor, which is the opposite of a cold-floor complaint.

options.a: Emergency egress illumination meets life-safety code minima and is separate from WELL circadian design goals
options.b: Emergency egress illumination is counted toward WELL circadian lighting targets whenever it runs continuously
options.c: Emergency lighting must meet the same melanopic targets as task lighting during normal occupancy hours
options.d: Egress illumination levels are set by WELL Light features rather than by local life-safety codes

distractorExplanations.b: Egress lighting is a life-safety system; it is not counted toward circadian targets for regularly occupied spaces.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergency lighting is governed by life-safety codes; melanopic targets apply to regular lighting design.
distractorExplanations.d: WELL does not set egress levels; building and life-safety codes establish minimum emergency illumination.

well-ap-readiness-check-light-movement-t.explanation: Life-safety emergency lighting satisfies code egress requirements; WELL Light addresses regularly occupied spaces and circadian strategies under normal operations. WELL circadian goals apply to lighting for regular occupancy, not life-safety egress lighting.

options.a: Ergonomic assessments of workstations performed once during the initial fit-out
options.b: Height-adjustable desks provided on request through the facilities team
options.c: Employer-supported physical activity programs or subsidies for fitness participation
options.d: Healthy vending standards that limit sugary drinks near fitness spaces

distractorExplanations.a: A one-time ergonomic check is a workstation measure, not ongoing programming that promotes physical activity.
distractorExplanations.b: Adjustable desks are a built amenity; the question asks for programming beyond physical amenities.
distractorExplanations.d: Vending standards are a Nourishment policy; they do not provide physical activity programs or incentives.

options.a: Higher melanopic light at the eye, which meets the circadian lighting requirement alone
options.b: Reduced overall lighting power density, which WELL counts as a visual comfort metric
options.c: Improved individual visual comfort and appropriate task illuminance at the workstation
options.d: Lower glare from daylight at the window, since task lights balance window luminance

distractorExplanations.a: Task lights aim at the work surface; circadian requirements depend on vertical light at the eye from broader sources.
distractorExplanations.b: Lighting power density is an energy metric; WELL visual comfort concerns illuminance, glare and occupant control.
distractorExplanations.d: Daylight glare is managed with shading; a desk task light does not counter bright window luminance.

options.a: Compliant handrails, contrast cues, and consistent tread dimensions for safe everyday use
options.b: Open-riser stairs with glass treads that make the stair more visible from the lobby
options.c: Wider landings with seating, while handrails are provided on one side to save space
options.d: Spiral stairs that fit a smaller footprint near the elevator lobby for daily use

distractorExplanations.b: Open risers and glass treads create tripping and visibility hazards that conflict with accessible, safe stair use.
distractorExplanations.c: Accessible stairs need handrails on both sides; seating on landings does not replace that safety requirement.
distractorExplanations.d: Spiral stairs have uneven tread depths that are hard for many users, conflicting with consistent tread dimensions.

options.a: Clothing insulation values, since larger groups tend to wear heavier clothing
options.b: Internal sensible heat gain and metabolic load from additional occupants
options.c: Radiant asymmetry from the conference room's exterior glazing
options.d: Outdoor-air supply temperature delivered by the central AHU

distractorExplanations.a: Group size does not change clothing; the fivefold rise in occupants mainly adds internal heat gain.
distractorExplanations.c: The glazing did not change between scenarios; the variable that changed is the number of people in the room.
distractorExplanations.d: Supply air temperature is unrelated to the occupancy change; added people raise sensible and metabolic heat load.

options.a: Visual discomfort, headaches, or performance issues for sensitive occupants
options.b: Shifted circadian phase caused by the blue spectral content of the flickering light
options.c: Lower color rendering that makes skin tones and materials appear unnatural
options.d: Reduced melanopic lux readings at the eye during working hours

distractorExplanations.b: Flicker is a temporal light artifact; circadian phase shift depends on melanopic dose, not flicker frequency.
distractorExplanations.c: Color rendering is a spectral property of the source and is separate from temporal flicker.
distractorExplanations.d: Flicker does not lower average melanopic light; its effects are discomfort, headaches and reduced visual performance.

options.a: Shift Movement efforts to remote-work fitness stipends and scale back on-site active design features
options.b: Consolidate amenities beside desks so in-office days are spent on focused, collaborative work
options.c: Lock interior stairs on low-occupancy days to reduce security and cleaning costs
options.d: Design the office to maximize active circulation and stairs for days when occupants are present

distractorExplanations.a: Removing on-site features loses activity benefits on office days; the design should still promote movement then.
distractorExplanations.b: Placing amenities beside desks reduces walking on the days occupants are present, which works against Movement.
distractorExplanations.c: Locked stairs push people to elevators and undermine habitual stair use, whatever the occupancy level.

options.a: High melanopic lux, tunable spectrum, and dimming at night for circadian support
options.b: Maximum daylight autonomy, large windows, and clear glazing on every facade
options.c: Appropriate illuminance, glare control, and color quality for tasks and spaces
options.d: Uniform 500 lux everywhere with 4000 K lamps and no individual controls

distractorExplanations.a: These are circadian lighting elements; visual comfort covers illuminance, glare control and color quality.
distractorExplanations.b: More daylight without glare control can reduce visual comfort; daylight quantity is not the same as comfort.
distractorExplanations.d: A single level ignores differing task needs and glare; visual comfort tailors illuminance to tasks and spaces.

options.a: Supply-air temperature at the AHU discharge only
options.b: Relative humidity at the return-air grille near the ceiling
options.c: Temperature and air speed at breathing zone and ankle level
options.d: CO2 concentration at the underfloor plenum outlet

distractorExplanations.a: AHU discharge temperature does not show stratification in the room; it must be checked at occupant heights.
distractorExplanations.b: Ceiling-level humidity does not reveal the vertical temperature gradient seated occupants feel between head and ankles.
distractorExplanations.d: CO2 at the floor outlet is a ventilation indicator; UFAD comfort issues are temperature gradients and drafts.

options.a: Daylight factor measured at a single point under a CIE overcast sky at the work plane
options.b: Annual sunlight exposure or related cumulative daylight metrics used with sDA/ASE frameworks
options.c: Unified Glare Rating calculated for each luminaire in the occupied zone across the working year
options.d: Equivalent Melanopic Lux measured at the eye at 9 a.m. on a set date each season

distractorExplanations.a: Daylight factor is a static point ratio under one sky, not a cumulative annual exposure metric.
distractorExplanations.c: UGR rates discomfort glare from electric luminaires and does not track daylight hours over the year.
distractorExplanations.d: EML is a point-in-time circadian measure at the eye, not an annual cumulative daylight metric.

options.a: Making active workstations accessible to all rather than treating movement as an exception
options.b: Reducing furniture procurement cost by buying a single desk type for the whole floor
options.c: Meeting ergonomic requirements, which WELL treats as a Thermal Comfort feature
options.d: Requiring standing work for set periods each day to meet a minimum activity target

distractorExplanations.b: Procurement savings are not the principle; default provision removes barriers to active working for everyone.
distractorExplanations.c: Ergonomics belongs to the Movement concept in WELL v2, not Thermal Comfort.
distractorExplanations.d: Default access offers choice; mandating standing time is a compliance rule, not universal support for movement.

options.a: Rely on the contractor's start-up report and keep the original setpoints unchanged for the first year
options.b: Run a single occupant survey before the retrofit and use it as the post-retrofit comfort baseline
options.c: Widen heating and cooling deadbands after handover to reduce energy use while complaints are logged
options.d: Commission controls, verify setpoints and schedules, and gather occupant feedback during seasonal changeover

distractorExplanations.a: A start-up report does not verify seasonal operation, and fixed setpoints ignore feedback after the retrofit.
distractorExplanations.b: A pre-retrofit survey cannot show how the new system performs; feedback must be gathered after changeover.
distractorExplanations.c: Widening deadbands trades comfort for energy without verifying controls, the opposite of comfort maintenance.

options.a: Bright morning daylight exposure followed by dim, warm lighting in the evening
options.b: Dim indoor days with very bright screens at night and little morning daylight
options.c: Perimeter desks with controlled daylight and automated shades for glare
options.d: Regular outdoor lunch breaks with moderate indoor lighting in the afternoon

distractorExplanations.a: This is a healthy pattern: strong morning light and dim evenings reinforce circadian alignment.
distractorExplanations.c: Controlled daylight at perimeter desks provides daytime light exposure that supports circadian alignment.
distractorExplanations.d: Midday outdoor light adds strong circadian stimulus; this pattern lowers rather than raises misalignment risk.

options.a: Equipment cut sheets showing chiller capacity, submitted without setpoint or survey information
options.b: An energy model showing annual HVAC consumption, which WELL accepts as proof of comfort performance
options.c: A single thermostat photo at handover showing a setpoint within the ASHRAE 55 range
options.d: HVAC design narratives, control sequences, and measurement or survey records demonstrating comfort criteria

distractorExplanations.a: Capacity data shows what equipment can do, not whether occupants are comfortable or criteria are met in operation.
distractorExplanations.b: Energy models estimate consumption; they do not demonstrate thermal comfort criteria for WELL verification.
distractorExplanations.c: A setpoint photo is not a design narrative, control sequence, measurement or survey record of comfort.

options.a: High-performance glazing with spectrally selective properties and exterior shading tuned by orientation
options.b: Clear single glazing on every facade to maximize daylight, with interior blackout blinds for the summer months
options.c: Dark-tinted glazing with low visible transmittance on each facade to cut solar heat gain and glare
options.d: A larger window-to-wall ratio on the west facade with interior shades to manage afternoon heat

distractorExplanations.b: Single clear glazing causes heat loss and solar gain, and blackout blinds remove daylight when closed.
distractorExplanations.c: Dark tints cut daylight as well as heat, sacrificing the Light benefit that spectrally selective glass keeps.
distractorExplanations.d: Interior shades absorb heat inside the envelope, and more west glazing increases low-angle glare and overheating.

options.a: Offer EAP counseling but require manager approval before employees can book a session
options.b: Provide mental health resources through HR only after a formal performance concern
options.c: Communicate leadership support for mental health resources and normalize use of EAP counseling
options.d: Run an annual resilience webinar while keeping EAP details out of internal communications and onboarding

distractorExplanations.a: Manager approval removes confidentiality and discourages help-seeking, which reinforces stigma.
