distractorExplanations.b: Linking support to performance problems frames help-seeking as disciplinary and deters early use.
distractorExplanations.d: A yearly webinar without visible resources does not normalize EAP use or signal leadership support.

options.a: A shared break room with a television and vending machines next to the main kitchen
options.b: A dedicated restorative room with comfortable seating, adjustable lighting, and acoustic privacy
options.c: An open lounge with bright overhead lighting located beside the reception desk
options.d: A bookable meeting room that is labelled as a quiet space whenever no meetings are scheduled in it

distractorExplanations.a: A busy break room with TV and kitchen noise lacks the acoustic privacy and calm needed for restoration.
distractorExplanations.c: High visibility, fixed bright light and reception traffic undermine the privacy and control restorative spaces need.
distractorExplanations.d: A part-time meeting room is not dedicated restorative space and is often unavailable when people need it.

options.a: A matching-gift program open to senior staff alone, with no volunteering component
options.b: An annual team-building retreat focused on internal collaboration skills
options.c: Paid volunteer time off paired with organized community service opportunities
options.d: Mandatory weekend volunteering tracked as part of performance reviews

distractorExplanations.a: Limiting the program to senior staff excludes most employees, and no volunteering component is offered.
distractorExplanations.b: Internal team-building builds collaboration but does not involve giving time or service to the wider community.
distractorExplanations.d: Making volunteering mandatory and unpaid undermines voluntary altruism and adds stress rather than benefit.

options.a: A ramped side entrance at the loading dock while the main public entrance keeps its steps
options.b: A level or ramped entry with adequate clear width and maneuvering space at the door
options.c: A level entry with a 28-inch clear door width and a manual door with a knob handle
options.d: A ramp at a 1:8 slope leading to the main entrance without handrails or landings

distractorExplanations.a: Universal design favors an equitable main entry; routing wheelchair users to a loading dock is segregating.
distractorExplanations.c: A 28-inch clear width is below the common 32-inch minimum, and knob hardware is hard to operate.
distractorExplanations.d: Accessible ramps are typically limited to a 1:12 slope with handrails and landings; 1:8 is too steep.

options.a: Documented procedures for evacuation, shelter-in-place, and occupant communication during emergencies
options.b: A list of emergency contact numbers posted at reception, with procedures to be written after occupancy
options.c: An evacuation map on each floor that covers fire exits but omits shelter-in-place and communications
options.d: A security-team protocol kept confidential so that occupants are not alarmed by drills or notices

distractorExplanations.b: Contact numbers are one element; documented procedures must exist before occupancy, not be deferred.
distractorExplanations.c: Fire exit maps alone ignore shelter-in-place scenarios and occupant communication, which a full plan covers.
distractorExplanations.d: Occupants must know procedures to respond safely; a confidential protocol leaves them unprepared.

options.a: Send an annual newsletter from management announcing policy changes after decisions are made
options.b: Restrict the shared event space to the anchor tenant, which hosts its own community programs
options.c: Publish a suggestion email address that the property team reviews once each year
options.d: Host regular forums where occupants can provide input on building policies and community initiatives

distractorExplanations.a: One-way announcements after decisions give occupants no input, which is the core of civic engagement.
distractorExplanations.b: Limiting space to one tenant excludes other occupants from participation in a multi-tenant building.
distractorExplanations.c: An inbox reviewed annually offers no dialogue or timely response, so it does not meaningfully engage occupants.

options.a: Wayfinding and health information signage in primary languages spoken by the occupant population
options.b: English signage with an on-call phone interpreter available at the reception desk during clinic hours
options.c: Multilingual signage limited to the main entrance, with English-only signs inside the clinic
options.d: Pictogram signage without any text, designed so that no single language is favored

distractorExplanations.b: An interpreter helps at reception, but English-only signs still leave many users unable to navigate or read health information.
distractorExplanations.c: Translated signs at the door alone leave wayfinding and health information inside inaccessible to many users.
distractorExplanations.d: Pictograms help but cannot convey detailed health information; signs should include the users' primary languages.

options.a: Detailed directory boards at the main entrance listing every room number
options.b: Consistent color-coded paths with simple landmark references at decision points
options.c: Alphanumeric room codes on small signs, with printed maps available at the front desk
options.d: Uniform corridor finishes so the building appears calm and visually simple

distractorExplanations.a: A long directory at the entrance relies on memory and reading; cues are needed at each decision point.
distractorExplanations.c: Abstract codes and maps held at a desk add cognitive load rather than giving simple cues along the route.
distractorExplanations.d: Identical finishes remove landmarks that help people with cognitive disabilities recognize where they are.

options.a: Multi-stall men's and women's rooms with one accessible stall in each
options.b: An all-gender restroom located on the basement level, reachable by stairs alone
options.c: Single-user all-gender restrooms with accessible fixtures and clear signage
options.d: Single-user restrooms labeled by gender, with accessible fixtures in one

distractorExplanations.a: Gendered multi-stall rooms meet accessibility but do not provide an inclusive option for users of all genders.
distractorExplanations.b: An all-gender room reached only by stairs excludes wheelchair users, so it is not inclusive of all abilities.
distractorExplanations.d: Gender labels on single-user rooms limit who can use them, and only one has accessible fixtures.

options.a: Install nature-themed artwork in corridors and reserve perimeter offices with views for senior staff
options.b: Place artificial plants throughout the floor, since visual greenery gives the same restorative effect
options.c: Install a green wall in the ground-floor lobby, away from the floors where most staff work
options.d: Provide views to landscaped outdoor areas and incorporate living plants in regularly occupied spaces

distractorExplanations.a: Artwork offers indirect nature, and reserving views for senior staff leaves most interior workers without access.
distractorExplanations.b: Living plants and real outdoor views provide stronger restorative benefits than artificial greenery.
distractorExplanations.c: A lobby green wall is not in regularly occupied spaces, so high-floor workers rarely benefit from it.

options.a: Ensure occupants understand procedures and can respond safely, including people with disabilities
options.b: Measure how quickly the building empties, with occupants who need assistance excused from drills
options.c: Test the fire alarm panel and sprinkler system for code compliance without involving occupants
options.d: Train floor wardens on procedures while other occupants receive the plan by email after the drill

distractorExplanations.b: Excusing occupants who need assistance means their evacuation procedures are never practised or tested.
distractorExplanations.c: Equipment testing is a code task; drills exist so occupants learn and practise how to respond safely.
distractorExplanations.d: Emailing the plan afterward does not build occupant readiness; drills should involve occupants directly.

options.a: Minimum 36-inch clear passage width with passing spaces at intervals
options.b: Continuous handrails on both sides, with corridor widths set by egress occupant load
options.c: Thick carpet with cushioned underlay to reduce noise along the corridor route
options.d: Raised thresholds at each doorway to separate floor finishes between rooms

distractorExplanations.b: Egress widths are sized for evacuation capacity, not mobility-device passage and passing space requirements.
distractorExplanations.c: Thick, cushioned carpet raises rolling resistance for wheelchairs; firm, stable surfaces are needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Raised thresholds create level changes that obstruct mobility devices; transitions should be flush or beveled.

options.a: Training managers to diagnose mental health conditions and assign treatment plans
options.b: Offering an annual stress survey with results reported by employee name to managers
options.c: Providing a mindfulness app subscription as a substitute for EAP access and manager training
options.d: Training managers to recognize distress signs and refer employees to confidential resources

distractorExplanations.a: Managers should recognize and refer, not diagnose or treat, which requires qualified clinicians.
distractorExplanations.b: Named reporting breaks confidentiality and discourages honest answers; surveys should be anonymous.
distractorExplanations.c: An app can supplement support but does not replace access to confidential professional help or trained referral.

options.a: Mind — restorative spaces
options.b: Community — civic engagement
options.c: Movement — active design
options.d: Community — emergency preparedness

distractorExplanations.a: Restorative spaces support stress recovery; voter registration and neighborhood meetings are civic participation.
distractorExplanations.c: Active design concerns physical activity through the built environment, not hosting civic events on site.
distractorExplanations.d: Right concept, wrong feature: emergency preparedness covers plans and drills, not civic engagement activities.

options.a: A quiet decompression lounge separated from clinical alarms and foot traffic
options.b: A staff break area at the nurses' station so workers can still hear patient alarms
options.c: A rooftop smoking shelter with seating, lit by bright overhead floodlights
options.d: A shared cafeteria seating zone reserved for staff during peak visiting hours

distractorExplanations.b: Staying within earshot of alarms prevents psychological detachment, which is the point of decompression.
distractorExplanations.c: A smoking area exposes staff to smoke, and bright floodlights work against calm decompression.
distractorExplanations.d: Cafeteria seating remains noisy and public, so it lacks the separation from activity that recovery requires.

options.a: First aid supplies and a fire extinguisher, with contact lists stored on the shared drive
options.b: First aid supplies, flashlights, water, contact lists, and backup communication tools
options.c: Bottled water and non-perishable food, with occupants bringing their own first aid items
options.d: Flashlights and a battery radio, with first aid supplies kept off site at a sister office

distractorExplanations.a: Contact lists on a network drive may be unreachable during outages, and the kit lacks water and lighting.
distractorExplanations.c: First aid supplies belong in the kit; relying on individuals leaves gaps, and communication tools are missing.
distractorExplanations.d: Off-site first aid supplies are unavailable in an emergency, and the kit omits water and contact lists.

options.a: High visual contrast between walls, floors, doors, and signage
options.b: Uniform light-coloured finishes on walls, floors, and doors
options.c: Polished stone floors that reflect overhead lighting brightly
options.d: Small serif lettering on signs to keep the interior uncluttered

distractorExplanations.b: Uniform light finishes reduce contrast, making edges, doors and floors hard to distinguish for low-vision users.
distractorExplanations.c: Reflective glossy floors create glare that impairs vision and can be misread as wet or uneven surfaces.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-vision users need large, high-contrast, sans-serif lettering; small serif text reduces legibility.

options.a: Satisfies Thermal Comfort outdoor-space requirements for the summer months
options.b: Supports Mind nature access and provides a restorative break from indoor work
options.c: Meets Air quality requirements by filtering outdoor air through native plants
options.d: Replaces the need for indoor active furnishings under the Movement concept

distractorExplanations.a: A walking trail is a nature and restoration strategy; Thermal Comfort features address indoor conditions.
distractorExplanations.c: Outdoor plantings do not meet indoor air requirements, which rely on ventilation, filtration and source control.
distractorExplanations.d: A trail can support activity, but it does not substitute for active workstations and furnishings indoors.

options.a: Sound masking raised to higher levels inside assembly spaces
options.b: Higher-STC partitions between assembly rooms and corridors
options.c: Hearing loop (induction loop) systems in assembly spaces
options.d: Louder PA speakers in assembly spaces with no assistive link

distractorExplanations.a: Sound masking lowers speech intelligibility on purpose; raising it in assembly rooms makes listening harder for hearing-aid users.
distractorExplanations.b: STC upgrades block sound between rooms for privacy; they do not deliver speech to hearing aids or cochlear implants.
distractorExplanations.d: Turning up loudspeakers adds reverberant noise and still gives hearing-aid users no direct audio feed like an induction loop does.

options.a: Universal design through step-free routes at every entrance
options.b: Wayfinding with redundant, legible cues at decision points
options.c: Emergency preparedness through posted evacuation route maps
options.d: Active design prompts placed near elevators to encourage stair use

distractorExplanations.a: Step-free entrances address physical access to the building, not the icon and floor-number cues that help people orient themselves.
distractorExplanations.c: Evacuation maps belong to emergency preparedness; consistent icons and floor numbering at elevators support everyday wayfinding.
distractorExplanations.d: Point-of-decision stair prompts are a Movement strategy; the scenario describes orientation cues, not activity nudges.

options.a: Improved sleep through circadian lighting design at desks
options.b: Stronger civic engagement through volunteer time off
options.c: Lower sedentary time through scheduled activity breaks
options.d: Reduced chronic stress and improved work-life balance

distractorExplanations.a: Circadian lighting is a Light concept strategy; flexible work and email limits act on workload stress, not light exposure.
distractorExplanations.b: Volunteer time off supports civic engagement; the policy here limits after-hours demands to relieve chronic work stress.
distractorExplanations.c: Activity breaks target Movement outcomes; discouraging after-hours email targets stress and work-life balance.

options.a: Ergonomic support through adjustable workstation design
options.b: Circadian support through melanopic lighting in rest areas
options.c: Stress recovery through access to restorative rest
options.d: Tobacco cessation support through designated wellness zones

distractorExplanations.a: Adjustable workstations are a Movement ergonomics strategy; rest pods give fatigued occupants a place to recover.
distractorExplanations.b: Melanopic lighting targets belong to the Light concept; the pods exist for restoration, not for delivering a light dose.
distractorExplanations.d: Tobacco cessation is a separate Mind feature about quitting support; rest pods address fatigue and stress recovery.

options.a: Audible PA announcements during the outage, followed by a written debrief for occupants the next day
options.b: Email and intranet posts to occupants, relying on the building network staying online
options.c: Multi-channel alerts including visual alarms, text notifications, and audible announcements
options.d: Floor-warden verbal instructions backed by printed evacuation maps posted at elevators

distractorExplanations.a: A single audible channel excludes Deaf occupants, and a next-day debrief gives no real-time guidance during the outage.
distractorExplanations.b: Email and intranet depend on building power and networks that may fail in an outage, and they reach only connected users.
distractorExplanations.d: Verbal instructions do not reach Deaf occupants, and elevators are out of service in an outage; there is no visual or text alert.

well-ap-readiness-check-mind-community-0.explanation: Inclusive emergency communication uses redundant, accessible channels so all occupants—including those with hearing or vision limitations—receive timely instructions. Providing those alerts in accessible formats extends them to occupants with sensory or cognitive disabilities.

options.a: Integrative design through a project-team charrette on WELL feature goals
options.b: Health and wellness awareness through a lobby guide to WELL features
options.c: Civic engagement and inclusive representation in the built environment
options.d: Occupant survey feedback collected through post-occupancy questionnaires

distractorExplanations.a: Integrative design brings project stakeholders together to set health goals; it is not resident co-created art in the lobby.
distractorExplanations.b: Wellness awareness covers educational materials about health features, not participatory art that represents the neighborhood.
distractorExplanations.d: Occupant surveys gather satisfaction data after move-in; co-designing artwork with residents is civic engagement and representation.

options.a: Round knobs with a textured grip finish for improved hand traction
options.b: Thumb-press latch handles requiring a pinch-and-press motion to open
options.c: Lever handles operable with a closed fist and without tight grasping
options.d: Lever handles mounted at 60 inches above the floor for visibility

distractorExplanations.a: Texture does not remove the need to grasp and twist a knob, which is the barrier for people with limited hand strength.
distractorExplanations.b: A pinch-and-press latch demands fine finger strength; universal design calls for hardware usable with a closed fist.
distractorExplanations.d: Levers are right, but 60 inches is above accessible reach range (about 34–48 inches), so many users cannot operate them.

options.a: Stress management through workload planning training
options.b: Mental health education through manager training on stigma
options.c: Restorative programming through on-site mindfulness classes
options.d: Mental health support and access to professional resources

distractorExplanations.a: Stress management focuses on identifying stressors and planning workload changes, not on clinical counseling sessions.
distractorExplanations.b: Mental health education raises awareness and reduces stigma; confidential counseling is access to professional services.
distractorExplanations.c: Mindfulness classes are restorative programming; telehealth counseling provides professional mental health treatment.

options.a: Biophilic design using artwork to reduce patient stress
options.b: Landmark-based wayfinding to reduce reliance on text alone
options.c: Universal design through slip-resistant flooring at intersections
options.d: Emergency egress marking with photoluminescent floor strips

distractorExplanations.a: The artwork and floor changes are placed at intersections to aid navigation; stress reduction via nature is a different goal.
distractorExplanations.c: The distinct floor materials signal location for orientation; slip resistance is a safety property, not a wayfinding cue.
distractorExplanations.d: Photoluminescent strips guide evacuation in darkness; landmark art and materials support everyday wayfinding.

options.a: Paid volunteer days directed to a single company-selected charity with participation tracked by HR
options.b: Matching donations for employee gifts, with no hands-on volunteering or team involvement
options.c: Team-based volunteer projects with choice of cause and recognition of participation at all levels
options.d: Volunteer-hour quotas tied to performance reviews and annual bonus eligibility

distractorExplanations.a: Choosing one charity for everyone removes autonomy, which research links to the well-being benefit of prosocial activity.
distractorExplanations.b: Donation matching helps causes but lacks the social connection and active contribution that drive prosocial well-being.
distractorExplanations.d: Tying volunteering to reviews and bonuses makes it coercive, which undermines the intrinsic motivation behind altruism benefits.

options.a: A mix of bench, armchair, and height-varied seating with adjacent wheelchair spaces
options.b: Uniform armless benches spaced evenly along the atrium edges for consistent sightlines and circulation
options.c: Bariatric-rated chairs throughout the atrium in a single standard seat height
options.d: Fixed tiered seating with wheelchair spaces grouped at the rear of the atrium

distractorExplanations.b: Armless benches give no support for standing up and include no wheelchair spaces, so they do not serve diverse bodies.
distractorExplanations.c: Bariatric chairs help some users, but one seat height and no wheelchair spaces fail people of other sizes and mobility needs.
distractorExplanations.d: Grouping wheelchair spaces at the back segregates users, and fixed tiers offer no choice of seat type or height.

options.a: Health and wellness awareness through digital feature guides
options.b: Wayfinding and inclusive access to navigation information
options.c: Occupant survey collection through interactive lobby screens
options.d: Emergency preparedness through digital evacuation alerts

distractorExplanations.a: Feature guides educate occupants about health strategies; screen-reader kiosks give inclusive access to navigation.
distractorExplanations.c: Collecting survey responses is occupant feedback, while these kiosks help people find their way with accessible text.
distractorExplanations.d: Evacuation alerts serve emergencies; adjustable-text wayfinding kiosks support daily navigation for all users.

options.a: Reduced perceived stress and improved attention restoration through contact with nature
options.b: Improved thermal comfort through evapotranspiration cooling from large indoor planting walls
options.c: Lower indoor VOC levels through potted houseplants replacing mechanical ventilation
options.d: Higher melanopic light exposure through nature imagery displayed on screens

distractorExplanations.b: Biophilia research centers on psychological outcomes; plant evapotranspiration has a negligible effect on room thermal comfort.
distractorExplanations.c: Houseplants remove too little VOC at building scale to replace ventilation; that is a myth drawn from small sealed-chamber studies.
distractorExplanations.d: Nature imagery offers visual restoration but does not deliver a meaningful melanopic dose, which is a Light concept metric.

options.a: Backup power is sized to keep full HVAC and plug loads running during utility failures
options.b: Emergency lighting relies on daylight through perimeter windows during daytime utility failures
options.c: Occupants shelter in place until utility power is restored before any notification
options.d: Critical life-safety and communication systems remain functional during utility failures

distractorExplanations.a: Emergency power prioritizes life-safety and notification systems; carrying full HVAC and plug loads is not the stated principle.
distractorExplanations.b: Daylight does not reach stairs and interior corridors and is absent at night, so emergency lighting needs its own backup power.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting for utility power before notifying anyone leaves occupants uninformed; mass notification must work during the outage.

options.a: Mandatory resilience training that frames stress as an individual coping deficit
options.b: Annual mental health awareness week led by HR with no change in manager behavior
options.c: Leadership modeling openness about workload limits and encouraging help-seeking without retaliation
options.d: Confidential EAP access promoted in onboarding packets, with leaders staying silent about team workloads

distractorExplanations.a: Framing stress as a personal deficit shifts blame to staff; psychological safety depends on leaders making help-seeking safe.
distractorExplanations.b: A one-off awareness week without changes in leader behavior does not make employees feel safe to raise workload limits.
distractorExplanations.d: An EAP is a mental health service; without leaders modeling openness, the team culture of psychological safety is unchanged.

options.a: Movement fitness equipment and Thermal comfort zones
options.b: Community emergency resilience and Air ventilation
options.c: Materials site remediation and Sound outdoor noise
options.d: Community universal design and Mind nature access

distractorExplanations.a: A step-free plaza to a park provides accessible routes and nature contact, not fitness equipment or thermal zoning.
distractorExplanations.b: Emergency resilience and ventilation are unrelated to a step-free connection between the building and a public park.
distractorExplanations.c: Site remediation addresses contaminated ground and outdoor noise is an acoustic issue; neither describes an accessible park link.

options.a: Occupant survey through annual post-occupancy satisfaction feedback
options.b: Integrative design through a pre-design stakeholder charrette
options.c: Civic engagement through occupant participation in shared decisions
options.d: Health and wellness promotion through a monthly wellness newsletter

distractorExplanations.a: Surveys collect one-way feedback; a green team gives occupants an ongoing role in proposing and shaping decisions.
distractorExplanations.b: Integrative design charrettes happen during project planning with the design team, not as an ongoing occupant group.
distractorExplanations.d: A newsletter pushes information to occupants; the green team is participatory civic engagement in shared decisions.

options.a: Private lockable room with seating, sink, outlet, signage, and proximity to work areas
options.b: Private lockable room with seating and outlet, located beside a restroom for sink access
options.c: Curtained corner within the first-aid room with a chair and refrigerator
options.d: Lockable multi-faith room shared on a booking schedule, with seating but no sink

distractorExplanations.b: Relying on a restroom sink is unhygienic for handling breast milk; WELL expects a dedicated space with a sink in or near it, not a restroom.
distractorExplanations.c: A curtain gives no lockable privacy, and sharing a clinical first-aid room makes the space unavailable when it is needed.
distractorExplanations.d: A shared booked room with no sink limits access during the day and lacks the sanitation a lactation room needs.

options.a: Sleep disruption from evening exposure to blue-enriched office lighting
options.b: Sedentary behavior from extended screen time at fixed workstations
options.c: Social isolation from reduced in-person collaboration after hours
options.d: Chronic work-related stress and burnout risk from always-on culture

distractorExplanations.a: Evening lighting is a Light and circadian factor; limiting after-hours email targets work stress and burnout.
distractorExplanations.b: Sedentary time is a Movement concern; deadline training and email limits address chronic work-related stress.
distractorExplanations.c: Isolation relates to social connection; the policy reduces after-hours work demands that drive burnout risk.

options.a: Zero-step entrance with automatic door and level threshold at the primary path
options.b: Ramped secondary entrance with automatic door, signed from the main stair entry
options.c: Zero-step entrance at the main path with a heavy manual door and raised sill
options.d: Revolving main door with an adjacent swing door available on staff request

distractorExplanations.b: Routing wheelchair users to a secondary entrance segregates them; universal design puts step-free access on the primary path.
distractorExplanations.c: A heavy manual door and raised sill create force and trip barriers even though the approach itself is step-free.
distractorExplanations.d: Requiring staff assistance to use the swing door makes access dependent on others instead of equal by design.

options.a: Health and wellness promotion through a fitness challenge
options.b: Responsible labor practices through contractor wage audits
options.c: Altruism through meaningful community contribution
options.d: Housing equality through affordable unit set-asides on site

distractorExplanations.a: A fitness challenge promotes physical activity; donating skilled volunteer hours is contribution to the wider community.
distractorExplanations.b: Wage audits address labor practices in the supply chain, not employees volunteering with a housing nonprofit.
distractorExplanations.d: Housing equality concerns affordable units within the project itself; volunteering off site for a nonprofit is altruism.
